home.startTitle: The next letter comes from your assistant.
home.startBodyHtml:
Use our hosted service on Cloudflare for your own space and login credentials.
Self-host, and create your own space after starting the service.
home.startNote: Hosted service has no public signup yet; credentials are issued by us.
home.faq1Q: Does it work with just one assistant?
home.faq1A: Yes. Have it send reports and results to you — that is the complete first pattern. When you need teamwork later, connect more assistants and authorize hand-offs.
home.faq2Q: Will it run my assistants for me?
home.faq2A: No. Assistants keep working in their own runtimes. Waypost only keeps messages, libraries and hand-off records; when things run and when mail is collected is up to each runtime.
home.faq3Q: If I read it in the inbox, has the assistant handled it?
home.faq3AHtml: Not the same thing. Reading in the Dashboard never sends a receipt for an assistant. received means the client saved it reliably; processed means the client actively confirmed it finished processing.
home.faq4Q: Do all instances already enforce the new protections?
home.faq4A: The new version is implemented and verified locally. Older instances need an upgrade, key configuration and data migration to get the same protection.
guide.tocMain: Hand off to Muse for summary
guide.title: Connect first, then hand off.
guide.ledeHtml:
Start with one assistant's letter.
Then let Today, Instinct and Grok Bot hand results to Muse for summary.
guide.sLoginBodyHtml:
Hosted service: we give you a Dashboard address and login credentials. Open the address, enter the credentials, and step into the space prepared for you.

Self-hosted: start the service per section 7, open the local Dashboard, and enter with the login credentials in the data directory. For first use, click “New space”.

Login credentials guard the inbox. Connecting an assistant issues a separate connection credential, stored in the assistant's private settings.
guide.sConnectBodyHtml:
In the Dashboard click “Connect assistant” and give it a name. Starting with Muse is fine. The page shows its MCP address, connection credential and identity.

Assistants need HTTP MCP or HTTP API support to connect. Booking restaurants and checking flights run in their environment; Waypost handles receiving, keeping, and authorizing.

Save this connection info in the assistant's runtime:

Server address  <your service address>/mcp
Header          Authorization
Header value    Bearer <connection credential>

The raw connection credential is shown once. Save it on the spot. If lost, revoke the old connection and issue a new one. Load the Waypost Skill to help the assistant understand the usage.

Once connected, ask the assistant to confirm identity and permissions:

Through Waypost, show me my identity, the capabilities I can use, and the default recipient.

New connections can only send to you by default. To deliver to Muse or collect for Muse, see section 4.
guide.sFirstBodyHtml:
Ask the assistant to send a simple note:

Through Waypost, send the default recipient a message with subject “I'm connected” and body “Progress and results can go here from now on”.

Back in the Dashboard's “Inbox”: the default recipient is this space's user entry, so the first letter arrives for you.

With a single assistant this is already the complete pattern: let it send milestone results to you, and read them when you like.
guide.sMainH: 04 / Hand off to Muse for summary
guide.sMainBodyHtml:
Muse is the lead assistant. Today, Instinct and Grok Bot do their work and hand results to it.

  1. Let Muse collect. Under “Assistants → Connections & permissions”, issue a connection with “collect own messages” plus “confirm collect and process”, keeping send ability so it can report to you.
  2. Let the others deliver. Issue each assistant a connection allowed to send, pick Muse under “extra recipients”, and save it into each runtime.
  3. Name the recipient when sending. Address Muse by its Actor ID, found in its connection info. The default recipient stays you — new authorizations never change it.
  4. Ask Muse to collect and summarize. Muse organizes the other assistants' results, then sends one report to the default recipient. Whether it runs manually or on a schedule is up to its runtime.

The “Inbox” shows the report sent to you. Hand-offs between assistants are under “Manage → All messages”.

Issuing a new connection never revokes the old one. When narrowing permissions, save the new connection, update the config, then revoke the original.
guide.sSharingBodyHtml:
Attachments suit delivering a single file with a message. Memory sets suit keeping a group of living documents — work results, reference notes, open questions.

Under “Connections & permissions”, open upload plus library read/write for the assistant providing libraries, creating its own set when needed. Then issue Muse library-read ability, ticking exactly which sets it may read.

Sets keep history. Muse can read the new libraries and check back against the version from back then. Writing into another assistant's set needs its own write authorization.

Moving source files also needs the runtime to support HTTP file upload and download. After upload, the service compares byte size and SHA-256 and archives only on match; to change content, upload a new library.

Authorization formats are in the connection & authorization guide; library export and the runnable flow are in the full example.
guide.sResumeBodyHtml:
Each client tracks delivery progress independently. Muse reading a message never confirms for another client.

  • received: the client reliably saved what it got.
  • processed: the client explicitly reports it finished processing.

Reading in the Dashboard sends neither receipt. On a send-side disconnect, reuse the original request ID to query or resume the submission. The reference client already implements the resume flow.
guide.sSelfBodyHtml:
Needs Rust 1.91 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/mainline-org/waypost.git
cd waypost
cargo run --release -- init --data ./var
cargo run --release -- serve --data ./var

Open http://127.0.0.1:8787/dashboard and enter with the login credential in var/admin-secret, then create your own space first.

You are this service's operator. To serve others, create a space per person, generate per-space credentials under “User login credentials”, and hand them over.

The service only accepts local connections by default. For public use over the internet, configure HTTPS; Cloudflare, backup and key setup are in the deployment notes.

This guide follows the new Dashboard names and default permissions. Existing services need an upgrade for the new onboarding flow; old connections keep their permissions. Encryption and user isolation also need matching configuration plus migration of old data — see Data & privacy for the actual coverage.
privacy.ledeHtml:
Who can read content, which data is protected,
and which parts are still yours and your operator's to manage.
privacy.notice: This page describes what the new code provides. Existing instances need configuration plus data migration for the same protection; our hosted service states its own rollout, and self-hosters should check config and migration status.
privacy.sSpacesH: Each user gets their own space
privacy.sSpacesBodyHtml:
User login credentials only manage their own space. Assistants, messages, libraries, memories and cursors inside a space are bound to it; swapping URLs or guessing resource IDs never reaches another user's data.

Creating spaces, issuing login credentials and maintaining the service is the operator's job. Self-hosted, that is you; on our Cloudflare hosted service, that is us. The operator keeps global admin rights, including managing all spaces and maintaining keys.

User login credentials and assistant connection credentials are used separately. After a user login credential is rotated or revoked, the old credential and its login sessions stop working immediately.
privacy.sEncryptionH: Content stored encrypted, decrypted by the server
privacy.sEncryptionBodyHtml:
The new version protects stored content with standard hybrid encryption. Message bodies, attachments, full memory listings, and message subjects, file names, memory paths and metadata in the database are encrypted at rest.

Space, object and field identities feed encryption authentication. Ciphertext moved under another space or object simply won't decrypt; on tampering or key mismatch, the service refuses to read.

The server can still decrypt. That keeps Dashboard content checks and pre-publish privacy filtering working — and means trusting whoever operates the service. A compromised running service is outside storage encryption's protection.

Operational data like identities, display names, authorization relations, timestamps, sizes, content types and digests still lives in the database. Encryption doesn't hide network traffic sizes either.
privacy.sPermissionsH: Connections only get what you grant
privacy.sPermissionsBodyHtml:
Assistant credentials authorize by space, identity, operation and resource. Permission to read messages never silently grows into reading all memories; watching space activity never reaches unshared libraries.

Sending across assistants needs an explicit recipient authorization. Sharing memories names the set and splits read from write. You can revoke connection credentials you no longer use, cutting later access and publishing.
privacy.sFilteringH: The privacy check only stops what it recognizes
privacy.sFilteringBodyHtml:
Rules can be set on an assistant's send or collect path to redact or block emails, phone numbers, common service credentials, sensitive fields and custom text before publishing.

Rules only cover their configured detection scope — they can't catch every privacy detail in natural language. Images, PDFs and binary attachments that can't be checked are blocked from protected channels by default; confirm the content before allowing.

Local privacy rules never send source text to outside models. Audit records keep the rule, the fields and the hit counts — never the raw sensitive matches.
privacy.sHistoryH: Keep history, and manage it too
privacy.sHistoryBodyHtml:
Update policies never rewrite published content. Memory deletion is logical — history files and other clients' copies are not wiped automatically.

Operators can preview before clearing expired staging uploads and unpublished objects. Archived libraries and memory history stay; cleanup has reference checks plus lease protection and never deletes content in use.

Back up encryption keys separately from data backups. After upgrading an old deployment, migrate historical content first, then handle old plaintext objects and backups under the retention policy. Once a key is lost, content still sealed under it can't be recovered.
privacy.sSiteH: This site only introduces the product
privacy.sSiteBodyHtml:
The homepage uses Today, Instinct and Grok Bot results summarized by Muse as a sample — it sends no messages and reads no libraries from your service. This site has no login form, no analytics tracking scripts, and no third-party font requests.

The “Copy” buttons only write sample prompts to the clipboard. Real login, assistant connections and library storage all happen in the Waypost service you choose; the site's hosting platform still handles normal page visits.

case.restaurant.title: Booked the restaurant, handed the confirmation to Muse
case.restaurant.lede: Burnt Ends, Nov 6, 7pm for two, booked. Waypost keeps the message; Muse folds dietary and rebooking terms into the trip plan.
case.restaurant.bodyHtml:
You asked Instinct to book a one-Michelin-star restaurant while other assistants handle flights and the itinerary. Everything moves, but confirmations scatter across conversations.

One message keeps a clear result

Once booked, Instinct sends the result to Muse:

Burnt Ends booked: Nov 6, 7:00pm, table for two, movable to Sat 8:00pm. One guest avoids peanuts. Free cancellation until Wed noon — please fold into the trip plan.

From confirmation to trip plan

  1. Instinct delivers time, party size and dietary notes to Muse through its own connection.
  2. Waypost keeps the message. Even before Muse collects, the information sits in the inbox.
  3. Muse collects, then puts the booking together with flights and trip notes into one complete plan for you.
Instinct → Waypost keeps the confirmation → Muse builds the plan → you

What you can see clearly

Burnt Ends is reported booked by Instinct; flights still open. Muse lists done items apart from to-dos instead of blending every message into one “trip done”.

A successful submission only means the message is kept. Waypost never verifies the restaurant's real order; whether the booking stands follows the restaurant's confirmation.

Which permissions to open

Grant Instinct permission to send to Muse, naming Muse when sending. Muse needs collect and receipt abilities, keeping send so it can report to you. To deliver confirmation files, open attachment upload plus matching read permission.

Steps are in the lead-assistant setup guide.
case.flight-monitoring.title: Watch flights on a schedule, keep the options worth deciding
case.flight-monitoring.lede: Grok Bot checks prices on your schedule and hands in-budget flights and arrival times to Muse to organize.
case.flight-monitoring.bodyHtml:
You want to watch Singapore–Tokyo returns and stay within budget. Grok Bot checks on a schedule; Muse keeps flight options together with what's already settled.

Every round leaves a result

When Grok Bot finds candidates, it writes to Muse:

Outbound Nov 6, departs 09:40, lands 14:35 local, S$540. Cheapest return is Nov 13 at S$598 against a S$600 budget. Nothing ticketed yet — please record and remind me to decide.

Check, hand off, organize

  1. You arrange the check cycle, dates, route and budget in Grok Bot's runtime.
  2. Grok Bot hands this round's results plus sources to Waypost, addressed to Muse.
  3. Muse collects and, together with the rest of the trip, sorts out the qualifying candidates and what needs your call.
Grok Bot checks → Waypost keeps results → Muse lines up candidates → you decide

No need to re-find the conversation each time

Every result carries source and time. Muse can keep organizing along received messages, and you can verify the originals under all messages.

Prices, routes and alert thresholds are samples; real prices follow suppliers at check time. Check cycles run in each assistant's environment; Waypost keeps messages and libraries — it never checks prices on a timer, buys tickets, or verifies deals.

Which permissions to open

Grok Bot needs permission to send to Muse. Muse needs collect permission; with files attached, grant upload plus library-read ability too. Price alerts never include buying permission.

Start from the setup steps and send one real round of results into the inbox.
case.main-assistant.title: Several assistants work, Muse gives you one full report
case.main-assistant.lede: Today, Instinct and Grok Bot each deliver; Muse sorts out what is done and what needs your decision.
case.main-assistant.bodyHtml:
Instinct books the restaurant, Grok Bot watches flights, Today organizes the trip notes. You want one lead assistant across these results to tell you the overall progress.

Let results pass through one inbox

Today / Instinct / Grok Bot → Waypost → Muse → you

Other assistants each hold a connection identity and deliver to Muse under authorization. Waypost keeps the hand-off content; Muse collects from its own inbox and keeps processing.

What's in the summary

Muse can hand you a report like this:

Burnt Ends Nov 6, 7:00pm for two confirmed, movable to Saturday, dietary noted. Outbound 09:40 picked; three return candidates, cheapest Nov 13 at S$598 against a S$600 budget. Please fix the return date by Wednesday.

Connect first, then authorize explicitly

  1. Connect Muse, switching on collect, receipt and send abilities.
  2. Connect the other assistants, issuing connections allowed to send to Muse and naming Muse as recipient when sending.
  3. In each runtime, save the connections and ask Muse to collect, summarize, and report to you.

New connections only send to you by default. Adding permission to send to Muse never changes the default recipient on its own; issuing a new connection never revokes the old one.

Results stay yours

Reports Muse sends you land in the personal inbox; hand-offs between assistants can be verified under “Manage → All messages”. You can revoke connections to stop later access and publishing.

When Muse runs and collects is up to its runtime. Waypost processing receipts only describe the stage the client reported — never that an outside booking or purchase succeeded.

See the full setup steps.
case.shared-materials.title: Hand over the originals, keep the version from back then
case.shared-materials.lede: Trip notes and reference files are kept as a group, and edited prices keep their old versions. Muse reads with permission and can check back against history.
case.shared-materials.bodyHtml:
Today organized the trip notes; Grok Bot found flight candidates. Muse needs the source libraries — and to know when they changed.

Keep working as one set of libraries

Keep trip notes, reference sources and open questions in a library set. Every update leaves a version; Muse reads the current content with permission and can check back against the version from back then.

Today's libraries → Waypost keeps versions → Muse reads with permission and keeps organizing

Updates still leave the old copy findable

The new note moved the return from S$612 to S$598; the old version stays. While organizing the report, Muse can cite which version it used instead of guessing from same-named files whether anything changed.

Attachments suit delivering one file with a message; library sets suit keeping a group of living content.

Only open this round's libraries

The assistant providing libraries needs upload plus library-write ability. Muse gets read authorization for the named sets; touching another assistant's set needs its own write grant.

The service checks authorization by space and resource. Logical deletion of a library never wipes history versions or already-downloaded copies on its own.

See the library-sharing guide for the exact setup.
case.resume.title: Dropped halfway, the hand-off still connects
case.resume.lede: The sender recovers that submission — S$540 out, S$598 back — and Muse resumes delivery and processing from the saved progress.
case.resume.bodyHtml:
Grok Bot finished sending that round of price results — S$540 out, S$598 back — then the connection dropped before Muse collected. You want to resume the same work after recovery, not resend and reprocess.

The sender finds the original submission

The same send reuses the same request ID. After a disconnect, query the original submission result, confirm whether the letter is kept, then continue from the existing result — no resend, no fear of duplicates.

The collector keeps its own progress

Muse reliably saves received messages before confirming collect; only after processing does it explicitly report the processing stage. Different clients each keep their own progress — never confirming for each other.

Assistant resumes delivery → Waypost keeps the message → Muse resumes pickup → processing continues

What can be resumed

Waypost provides resume information for message and library hand-offs. The reference client implements reliable saving, confirming and restart recovery; other runtimes follow the same flow.

Reading a message in the Dashboard never sends a receipt for Muse, nor proves an outside action already finished.

See the drop-recovery notes and the runnable example.

rfc.noticeHtml: Body generated from repo docs, preserving original spec status and examples. Draft RFCs and validation plans may differ from the current implementation; verified scope is in the implementation record, and encryption plus user-isolation upgrades are in the security notes. Full text is currently Chinese-only; the English version is in progress.
rfc.indexTitleHtml:
To understand a hand-off,
start from its agreements.
rfc.indexLedeHtml:
RFCs define Waypost's public behavior: goals, contracts, state transitions, failure semantics and validation properties.
Full text is kept here, with draft spec and actual implementation records marked apart.
rfc.card0001Desc: Identity & authorization, message delivery, independent collecting, receipts, library sealing, memory versions and failure semantics.
rfc.card0002Desc: Operator Dashboard, content checks, login & sessions, plus the permissions and information boundaries of operator actions.
rfc.card0003Desc: Pick policies per participating agent: check text, libraries and metadata before publishing, and keep a security audit.
rfc.cardPropertiesDesc: Validation contracts for space isolation, idempotency, publish recovery, independent consumers, CAS and controlled faults.
rfc.cardValidationDesc: Tests actually run, local and Cloudflare acceptance, and the production edges still unverified.
rfc.cardSecurityDesc: User management isolation, server-side encryption, key configuration, old-data migration and security cleanup.
rfc.noteBodyHtml:
Drafts are the implementation baseline, not a promise that every ability is live. When observable behavior or permission meanings change, version and migration notes ship with it; implementation state is confirmed through property tests and real acceptance.

The site is generated from repo docs, keeping source content and status. Diagrams keep their Mermaid source and the raw Markdown downloads; where implementation differs, validation and security notes rule.
